Cells measure orders credited to the column, not orders that happened. A green cell can mean the row channel created demand the column got the click for. A red cell most often means the same order still happened but resolved to a different last click — not that spending in one place destroyed sales in another. There are red cells here; all are small, all sit low among the surviving pairs, and none has a mechanism this data can confirm. Click one to see the case against it.

What the caused customers are worth

Reallocating orders changes what they are worth, because orders are not interchangeable. Twelve-month gross profit per customer runs from to depending on where the customer came from, so a channel shown to drive orders into a better-retaining destination gains more value than the order count alone suggests — and one being credited for other people’s orders may be losing better customers than it keeps.

What this changes

How this was worked out

Weekly changes, two-week effects, promotions, and what the method cannot do

The problem. Every budget rises and falls together with demand, so a naive comparison of Meta spend against TikTok Shop revenue mostly measures "the business had a good week". Everything here is estimated with all ten spend channels in one model, so each effect is what remains once the others are held still. Promotional depth, gift-with-purchase, November/December and two Fourier seasonal terms are also held still.

Promotions never stop, which limits what can be asked. A promotion ran on every single day of this window — not most days, all of them. So there is no unpromoted baseline anywhere in the data, and nothing here can answer what sales would look like without discounting. What does vary is promotional depth, and that is what the model controls for. It matters: weekly changes in promo depth correlate with weekly changes in total ad spend at r = 0.39, so a model that ignored promotions would credit ad channels for discounting.

Weekly changes, not levels. Spend and results both trend upward over four years, and correlating two rising lines invents a relationship. Everything is estimated on week-to-week changes. Standard errors are Newey-West, which stops repeated weeks being counted as independent evidence.

How much data this rests on. weeks, and that is not a lot for a model of this size. Excluding November and December removes about twenty-two of them and costs far more than the count suggests, because the holiday weeks contain much of the spend variation the model learns from. The number of pairs clearing the bar drops sharply as a result. That is a power loss rather than a refutation, but it does mean few of these findings are robust to the strictest reading, and any pair that changes verdict between the two settings should be treated as unresolved rather than resolved in whichever direction is convenient.

From a weekly rate to a yearly number. Every coefficient describes one more $1,000 a week. The table reports annual orders, and bridging the two means choosing how large a change to price. Pricing the whole budget — down to spending nothing — is beyond anything the data saw and produces impossible answers. So each flow is sized at that channel dropping from its average week to its quietest week in this window: interpolation inside the observed range rather than extrapolation past it. Every total here is consequently a floor, and switching a channel off would move more credit than shown.

Credit moves, it is not created. Orders taken from one channel are handed to another, so the two sides of the ledger are the same sum written twice and the order total is unchanged by the reallocation. The foot of the table recomputes both sides for whichever view is showing and reports any difference, because that identity has been broken once by a channel silently dropping off the table.

Two questions, kept separate. Whether an effect exists at all, and how much of it is real. Answering them with one number was tried and made the results worse, so they are answered independently.

Does it exist? Judged against shuffled data rather than a formula. The usual false-discovery correction on standard errors turned out to be far too generous here: tested on data where each spend series had been circularly shifted so no real link could exist, it still declared about six pairs significant per run against the one it promised. Weekly business series share so much seasonal structure that ordinary standard errors understate how easily a coincidence clears the bar. So each spend series is shifted at random 250 times, the whole model refitted each time, and a pair has to beat what that same pair produced on shuffled data. The bar therefore differs by pair, from roughly 1.9 to 5.5, rather than one threshold for everything.

How much of it is real? Measured against a second market. International sees the same demand, the same promotions and the same seasonality, but a different amount of each channel's money. Regress US spend against International orders, where it cannot act, and any coefficient that appears is shared timing rather than effect. The share of the original it represents is subtracted, and the pair keeps the remainder. Nothing is all-or-nothing: Television keeps 99% of its effect on CRM SMS and 52% of its effect on Google Search.

Why that can be trusted. Television and TikTok Shop spend nothing at all internationally, so for those two the comparison market is genuinely untreated and the measurement is a clean placebo with a known answer. The method reproduces all 22 of those answers exactly. For channels running in both markets the comparison is imperfect and reads about twelve points stricter than a cleaner one would — the strict version was kept because the looser one broke the calibration.

Negative effects are excluded from the reallocation. Not by the statistics, which are blind to sign, but by an accounting rule: a channel suppressing another channel's orders is not credit changing hands, so there is nobody to move it from. Those pairs are reported in the matrix and left out of the ledger.

Two weeks, counted together. Advertising does not resolve inside a calendar week, and a same-week-only reading gets two things wrong: it misses effects that arrive late, and it credits spend for purchases it merely brought forward. Every figure here is therefore the cumulative effect across the week of the spend and the week after, estimated jointly. Where the second week is negative, that subtraction is already inside the headline number. The detail panel shows the split.

The backwards test. A real effect cannot work backwards, so each pair is re-run asking whether this week's spend explains last week's results. It should find nothing; where it finds something, the pair is flagged amber, because that pattern means both series are being driven by something the model has not captured.

Measured alone, versus measured properly. Every pair is also estimated the naive way — that one spend series against that one result, nothing held still. The detail panel shows both. The gap between them is what a single-channel reading would have wrongly credited to the channel, and it is usually large.

What this still is not. Observational evidence. Holding a channel still in a model is not the same as switching it off. A spillover here can also mean credit moving rather than demand appearing: Meta causes a purchase that arrives via Direct and is recorded as Direct. That matters for deciding where budget goes, but it is not new demand. The only way to settle a specific channel is to withhold it and watch.

Appendix — every calculation, worked through

One pair is followed from the raw weekly rows to the final adjusted cost, with the actual arithmetic at each step. The pair is Meta spend → CRM Email orders, on the default view: all regions, orders, holidays included. Every other cell on the page is produced by the identical procedure.

1. The panel

One row per week per region, built from agg_master.custom_sessions_orders_spend at daily grain and summed to weeks. Weekly rather than daily because ad spend and orders do not land on the same day; weekly rather than monthly because the model needs more observations than it has predictors, and monthly would give about 25 rows against 18 of them. Window: Aug 2024 to Jul 2026, of which 101 weeks survive differencing and lagging.

Six consecutive rows from the middle of the panel.

2. Differencing

Both columns trend upward across the window. Correlating two rising series measures the fact that they rise, not that one moves the other. So every column is converted to its week-on-week change before anything else happens:

Δyt = yt − yt−1

Applied to the rows above — the week of 2024-10-21 becomes $110,413 of extra spend and 105 extra orders:

WeekΔ Meta spendΔ CRM Email orders
2024-10-21$110,413105
2024-10-28$-91,109411
2024-11-04$23,639-75
2024-11-11$524,7576,815
2024-11-18$-70,974-2,529

This also removes, for free, anything constant across the window: brand equity, price architecture, the customer base, the fact that email volume is structurally larger than TikTok's. None of those need measuring, because a constant differences to zero.

The block rule. When holidays are excluded, November and December are cut out, leaving a hole in the calendar. Differencing across that hole would compute an eleven-week change and label it a one-week change. Differences are therefore taken within contiguous runs only, and the first row after any gap is dropped rather than differenced across it. The same rule governs the lag introduced next.

3. Two weeks, counted together

Advertising does not resolve inside a calendar week. A same-week-only model gets two distinct things wrong: it misses effects that arrive late, and it credits spend for purchases it merely pulled forward from the following week. Both are fixed by estimating the cumulative effect across the week of the spend and the week after.

The natural way to write that is a coefficient on this week's spend and another on last week's, with the answer being their sum. But then the quantity of interest has no standard error of its own. So the model is reparametrised to put the sum directly on one term. For each channel j, two regressors are built:

sj,t = Δspendjt     qj,t = Δspendjt−1 − Δspendjt

This is an identity, not an approximation — βΔst + φΔst−1 rearranges to (β+φ)st + φqt. The coefficient on s is therefore the full two-week effect, with its own honest standard error, and the coefficient on q is the second week's share of it. That second coefficient is what the panel reports as “of which week two”; where it is negative, the subtraction has already happened inside the headline figure.

4. The model

For a destination d, one equation is fitted across all 101 weekly changes at once:

Δordersdt = α + ∑j ( βj sj,t + φj qj,t ) + γ1Δpromo deptht + γ2Δpromo dayst + γ3ΔGWPt + γ4ΔNov/Dect + ∑k=1,2(δkΔsin 2πkw/52 + δ'kΔcos 2πkw/52) + εt

Spend is in thousands, which is why every coefficient reads “per $1,000 a week”. 10 channels contribute two terms each, plus 7 controls and an intercept. The two sine/cosine pairs are a Fourier seasonality term — they trace an annual and a half-annual wave, absorbing recurring calendar shape without spending 52 parameters on week dummies.

Solved by ordinary least squares, the closed form minimising squared error:

β̂ = (X'X)−1X'y

where X holds the differenced predictors and y the differenced CRM Email order changes. The spend block of the solution:

Read it as: holding the other 9 budgets, promotions and seasonality still, $1,000 more Meta spend is followed by about 2.9 more orders credited to CRM Email across the two weeks. The week-two component is -1.57, so the same-week figure alone would have been 4.50 — the second week gives some back, and the headline is already net of it.

5. The standard error

Plain OLS assumes each week is independent evidence. Weeks are not — a good stretch of trading persists, so errors are autocorrelated and treating them as independent overstates certainty. Standard errors are Newey–West (HAC) with a four-week bandwidth, which reweights the covariance matrix by how much neighbouring residuals actually co-move:

V̂HAC = (X'X)−1 [ ∑t et2xtxt' + ∑l=14 wl ∑t etet−l(xtxt−l' + xt−lxt') ] (X'X)−1,   wl = 1 − l/5

Here the naive OLS error is 1.34 and the HAC error is 0.99. From there:

t = 2.927 / 0.995 = 2.94  →  p = 0.00326

And the 90% range printed in the panel is the coefficient plus and minus 1.645 errors:

2.93 ± 1.645 × 0.99 = 1.29 to 4.56

6. Why “measured alone” is bigger

Run the same regression with Meta as the only channel and the coefficient is 9.47 instead of 2.93. The gap is not noise; it is arithmetic. A regression omitting a correlated variable absorbs that variable's effect in proportion to how strongly the two move together:

β̂alone = βMeta + ∑j≠Meta βj × δj

where δj is what you get regressing term j on Meta's spend term — how much of j moves when Meta moves. Every term, including the week-two components:

7. The backwards test

The regression is refitted with the result series moved one week earlier, asking whether this week's spend explains last week's orders. Nothing acts backwards in time, so a significant answer means both series are riding something the model has not captured, and the pair is flagged amber rather than counted. Result here: coefficient -2.84, p = 0.143. Above 0.05, so passed.

The forward direction is no longer a separate test, because the two-week model already contains it. A pair whose second week reverses is not disqualified — its headline number is simply smaller, having had the reversal netted out.

8. Testing 130 pairs at once

At a flat 5% threshold, 130 tests would throw up about 6 apparently-real results from pure noise. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls the share of false positives among the pairs declared real: sort all p-values ascending and find the largest rank i satisfying

p(i) ≤ 0.05 × i / 130

That largest rank is 58, giving a working cutoff of p ≤ 0.0135 — about 27% of the naive threshold. 58 of 130 pairs clear it. This pair ranks 3th with p = 0.00326.

9. What the scatter plot actually shows

A coefficient from a 18-parameter model cannot be plotted directly on two axes. The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem gives the equivalent picture: regress the spend term on everything else and keep the residual; regress the result column on everything else and keep the residual; the simple slope between those two residuals equals the multivariate coefficient exactly.

x̃ = sMeta − fitted(sMeta | all other terms)
ỹ = ΔordersCRM Email − fitted(ΔordersCRM Email | all other terms)
slope(ỹ ∼ x̃) = 2.9265568277  =  β̂Meta = 2.9265568277 ✓

Identical to ten decimal places. The dots are not a simplified illustration of the finding — they are the finding, drawn. Because the reparametrisation put the two-week total on a single regressor, this remains true even though the effect spans two weeks.

10. From a weekly rate to a yearly number

A coefficient says what one more $1,000 a week does. The table at the top of the page reports annual orders. Getting from one to the other is the step where this analysis previously went wrong, so it is worth setting out carefully.

The naive conversion is to multiply the rate by the whole budget:

2.93 × ($979,123 / 1,000) × 52 = 149,004 orders a year   ✗

That silently asks what would happen if Meta spent nothing. Meta’s average week is $979,123 — nearly a thousand steps of $1,000 — and the model only ever watched the budget move inside a band of roughly $0.5M to $1.7M a week. Projecting a local slope a thousand steps down to zero is not something the data can support, and it showed: applied across every channel, the arithmetic produced negative annual orders for Direct and CRM SMS, because the credit it claimed to move exceeded everything attribution had ever given them. An impossible answer is a useful one.

The fix is to price the flows at a change that actually happened. Each channel is taken from its average week down to its quietest week in the window. For Meta that is a pullback of $461,663 a week rather than the full $979,123:

Meta → CRM Email = 2.93 × ($461,663 / 1,000) × 52 = 70,256 orders a year

Every flow in the table is built that way. It is interpolation inside the observed range instead of extrapolation beyond it, which is why no channel comes out impossible any more. The cost is that the numbers are floors: switching a channel off entirely would move considerably more credit than shown, and this analysis cannot say how much.

11. The ledger, and why it has to balance

A channel’s adjusted total is what attribution gave it, less the orders another channel drove into it, plus the orders it drove elsewhere:

A‑Orders = attributed − in + out
Meta: 835,527 + 8,638 in − 0 out = 844,165

Only positive spillovers take part. A positive coefficient means one channel earned orders another was credited for — moving them corrects a misplacement, and both halves of the entry are real. A negative coefficient means more spend at one channel goes with fewer orders credited to another, and there nobody was credited for the orders that failed to appear, so there is no counterparty to debit. Booking those as transfers charges a channel for volume it never held; in this data it left YouTube at minus 1,481 orders against nil attributed, which is not a possible state. Negative pairs are reported in the matrix and the detail panel and kept out of the ledger.

Note that the labels invert between the arithmetic and the display: what arrives as credit from elsewhere is subtracted, because those orders belong to whoever drove them. The table shows the two figures the way a channel experiences them — orders gained and orders lost — so the row reads left to right.

Summed across all channels, the two sides are the same quantity written twice: every order taken from one destination is an order handed to some source. So

∑channels in = ∑channels out = 124,262  →  total orders unchanged at 2,268,181

That identity is guaranteed by construction, which is exactly why it is worth checking rather than assuming. It broke once: a channel whose own spend fell below a display threshold was dropped from the table while still appearing in other channels’ flows, so orders left one row and arrived nowhere. The balance line at the foot of the table recomputes both sides on every view and reports the difference.

12. Cost, return and value from the adjusted total

Once the order count is settled, the rest is division:

A‑CAC = spend / A‑Orders = $50,914,403 / 844,165 = $60.31
A‑ROAS = adjusted revenue / spend    A‑CM = A‑Orders × $29.22 / spend    A‑AOV = adjusted revenue / A‑Orders

The marginal figures are kept underneath rather than displayed, and appear on hover: Meta’s marginal cost per order is $82.46 against the $60.31 average shown in the cell. The two differ because one prices the next order and the other prices all of them.

Customer value is applied where each order actually landed. Orders a channel keeps are valued at its own twelve-month gross profit; orders it gains are valued at the gross profit of the destination they were counted in, since that is where they were observed. That is what allows Meta’s blended customer value to exceed its own — the orders it turns out to be driving surface through channels that retain better.

Limitation. Contribution margin uses one blended rate per new order, so A‑CM is A‑Orders rescaled by a constant and will always tell the same story. Making it independently informative needs channel-level COGS, which this panel does not carry.

13. The holdout calculator

Everything above is statistical. To establish cause you have to turn the channel down and watch. The calculator inverts the standard two-sample power formula — 80% power at 5% significance needs the effect to be about 2.8 standard errors — to ask how many weeks that would take:

weeks ≥ 2 × ( 2.8σ / effect )2

σ is this pair's own residual noise, the standard deviation of the vertical axis on the scatter: 921 orders a week. At a 20% holdout:

spend withheld = $979,123 × 20% = $195,825/week
expected effect = 2.93 × (195,825 / 1,000) = 573 orders/week
weeks = 2 × (2.8 × 921 / 573)2 = 2 × 20 = 40 weeks

The relationship is quadratic, so doubling the holdout cuts the requirement fourfold. That is the lever, not patience.

14. What none of this establishes

All of the above is a careful correlation. Holding a channel still inside a model is not the same as switching it off, and no amount of controlling substitutes for an experiment. There is also no natural experiment hiding in this history to fall back on: across the window only YouTube shows meaningful on/off variation, so there is nothing resembling a clean before-and-after for the channels that matter.

Two specific cautions. First, extending the window from one week to two was not a cosmetic choice — it changed which pairs qualify and moved several adjusted costs materially. A result that depends on where the window stops is a result worth treating as provisional. Second, a spillover can mean credit moving rather than demand appearing: Meta causing a purchase that arrives via Direct and is recorded as Direct. That still matters for where budget goes, but it is not new demand, and only a holdout separates the two.

Appendix — the underlying data

Everything the analysis is built on, in readable form. The weekly panel is the actual model input; the monthly view is an aggregation of it for reading. Nothing here is seasonally adjusted — the model controls for seasonality with terms inside the regression rather than by altering the data first, so there is no adjusted variant to show.

Downloads


Channel summary

Spend, attributed new customer orders and revenue by channel, trailing twelve months against the twelve before. CAC and ROAS here are the channel’s own attributed figures — the adjusted versions are further up the page.

Monthly data

The correlation inputs, by calendar month and region.

Promotional calendar

Every day with a promotion running, in total — which is every day in the analysis window, without exception.

The regressions control for promotional depth and gift-with-purchase. They do not use the other fields here, and that is a tested decision rather than an oversight. Adding promotion type, structure, whether a code was required, deal-of-the-day presence, named-event days, how many promotions started in the week, and how far into a run each day sat produced no improvement: the same 21 pairs cleared the bar, adjusted R² moved from 0.783 to 0.787, and average standard errors got slightly worse because five extra parameters cost more precision than the new information bought. The richer detail is real, but 101 weekly observations cannot resolve it.

One field was removed after this check. “Promo days per week” had been a control, but since a promotion runs continuously it equals seven in every week — a constant, contributing nothing. Dropping it changed no coefficient in this analysis by any amount visible at fifteen decimal places, and the model is one parameter leaner for it.
